title: Probe-Guided Gradient Balancing for Multimodal Learning
claim: A decoupled probe-based monitor estimates each branch's quality and feeds a bounded gradient boost back to the weaker one without touching the loss.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right forward path, probe branch below, green feedback loop on top
description: A single block diagram of a two-modality (audio and visual) network. In the top half, the audio input x_a goes through Encoder f_a to give z_a, and the visual input x_v goes through Encoder f_v to give z_v. Both feed a concatenation node, then Classifier g, then a red loss box. Blue marks audio and orange marks visual. Below, stop-gradient copies sg[z] drop down to dashed green linear probes h_a and h_v, which output accuracies P_a and P_v. These feed a dashed green Boost block holding the relative-gap formula w_m and the EMA-smoothed scale update, clipped at s_max. A thick green line leaves this block, runs along the top, and returns to the encoders as scaled gradient boxes (gradient times s_m). A legend at the bottom explains the arrow colors.
caption: An Illustration of probe-guided gradient boosting on 2 modalities. Forward path (top): features zm are concatenated and classified via the shared fusion classifier g, producing L. Probe monitoring (bottom): stop-gradient features sg[zm] are evaluated by linear probes along solid per-modality probe-flow lines (audio in blue, visual in orange), yielding per-modality accuracies ¯Pm. The boost block computes the relative-gap weight wm and a smoothed scale ¯sm (EMA-smoothed, refreshed only at probe-evaluation events every K steps and held constant in between), clipped at smax. The actuation rail (thick green) applies ¯sm to the per-modality gradient ∇θmL. Probes never backpropagate into encoders, so the monitoring signal is structurally decoupled from the fusion objective.
abstract: Jointly trained multimodal networks frequently underutilize weaker modalities, as faster-learning modalities dominate the shared fusion objective and suppress gradients reaching slower ones. Most existing approaches throttle dominant modalities, whereas directly boosting weaker modalities often fails because monitoring signals derived from the joint loss remain dominated by stronger modalities. We propose Probe-Guided Gradient Boosting (PGGB), a gradient modulation approach that boosts weaker modalities while preserving the strength of dominant ones. PGGB attaches lightweight linear classifiers to stop-gradient features from each modality to estimate representation quality independently. The gap between these scores, termed the utilization gap, provides an imbalance signal used to adaptively scale weaker-modality gradients through bounded and smoothed modulation. PGGB is composable with throttling methods, as it leaves the loss function and fusion architecture unchanged. Experiments across eight benchmarks spanning four domains and 2-4 modalities demonstrate that PGGB outperforms state-of-the-art methods on highly imbalanced multimodal datasets while remaining competitive under low or negligible imbalance. We further establish bounded scaling, self-attenuation, and a descent bound for standard SGD under smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions. Code is available at https://github.com/VuVoCodes/PGGB.
